newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-NSW manufacturing still depressed - study.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-NSW manufacturing still depressed - study.

text.p: Manufacturers in New South Wales (NSW), Australia's most populous state, see a clear need for a further cut in official interest rates to boost employment, according to a survey released on Sunday.

The Australian Business Chamber-Colonial State Bank survey of manufacturing found that for the 9th consecutive quarter, manufacturers expected continued job shedding in the coming 12 months. The managing director of the Business Chamber, Phillip Holt, said the September quarter national accounts, released last week, gave an over-optimistic picture of manufacturing.
"Seaonally adjusted, our survey indicates the worst pre-Christmas business conditions in four years," he said in a statement released with the survey results.
Seasonally adjusted, general business conditions have declined for the past three quarters, and have been weak for the past two years, the survey found.
Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said that lower inflation and higher unemployment had occurred in the September quarter, as pointed to by the survey.
"The story is the same this quarter. Prices are static, if not falling, and firms are shedding labour."

NSW manufacturers expect to reduce employment by almost 3,000 jobs over the year -- which would mean potential job losses of 12,000 in Australian manufacturing in 1997, the study found. Kunnen said lower rates would ease cost pressures and boost consumer confidence, which manufacturers saw as lacking.
"Disappointingly, the normal boost to production and sales expected in the lead-up to the Christmas season has been lower than in previous years," he said.

Holt said the sector remained depressed, and could not create new jobs to reduce unemployment, something that needed to be considered by both the Reserve Bank and the Federal Government when deciding policy.
The survey also found that for the eighth consecutive quarter, more firms (37 percent) saw profits decline than those reporting rises (28 percent).
Manufacturing firms reported softer selling prices for the fifth consecutive quarter, with 17 percent of firms reporting a fall in selling prices and only 10 percent experiencing a rise.

The survey found that the proportion of firms operating above 70 percent capacity rose to 64 percent in the December quarter, level with the fourth quarter last year but well down on the level of the December 1994 quarter.

A seasonal upturn in December quarter production saw 35 percent of firms report higher production levels compared with 26 percent reporting lower, the first reported net increase in eight quarters. The outlook for the March quarter was more modest, however, with 23 percent of firms looking for an increase against 29 percent expecting a production fall.
Investment in plant and equipment is expected to slacken in the March quarter, the survey found.
The proportion of firms engaged in exporting remained at historically high levels in the December quarter and was expected to remain high, at around 58 percent of firms, in the March quarter.

The December quarter survey was the 48th in the series, and covered 505 manufacturing firms in NSW who between them employ nearly 126,000 people, or about 30 percent of the NSW manufacturing sector workforce.
